statement: To switch a relay coil, DC motor, or other inductive DC load from a microcontroller digital output, drive an NPN BJT (or N-channel MOSFET) as a low-side switch and place a reverse-biased diode directly across the coil; the diode conducts before a large voltage can form when coil current is interrupted.
condition: Load current exceeds the ~20 mA a GPIO can reliably source/sink; with the exception of some reed relays, very few relays switch with less than 50 mA, so a transistor stage is nearly always required for relays.
inputs: MCU digital output pin (5 V logic assumed; adapt for 3.3 V)
outputs: Switched current through relay coil / DC motor / solenoid (relay contacts then switch the high-power circuit)
required_blocks: NPN bipolar transistor with base resistor (Fig. 13.21 topology) OR N-channel MOSFET (Fig. 13.22 topology) as low-side switch
Flyback diode reverse-biased across the coil; general-purpose 1N4004 recommended; diode peak-current capability must be >= the maximum current that was flowing through the coil
Coil supply rail sized for coil current (relay coil driven within its rated control voltage)
design_notes: The same schematic (Fig. 13.23) controls DC motors; driving the digital output with PWM controls motor power/speed via duty cycle
All components must be selected according to current and voltage ratings
For bidirectional motor control use an H-bridge instead; IC H-bridges such as TB6612FNG suit motor currents under a couple of amps and often add thermal shutdown
For AC-actuated coils this diode approach does NOT work (see ac-coil-rc-snubber entry)

source.section: 13.5.3 High-Power Digital Outputs — Relays and Other Inductive Loads; 3.4.2/3.4.3 Relay notes and Relay Driver

statement: Wire a pushbutton between a digital input and GND with a pull-up resistor to the supply, so the pin reads HIGH until the switch closes and LOW when pressed (inverted logic); debounce the input, normally in software with a lockout period after the first transition.
condition: Any mechanical switch or button feeding an MCU digital input at 5 V logic (adapt values for 3.3 V).
outputs: Debounced logic level on MCU digital input (LOW = pressed for pull-up wiring)
required_blocks: Pull-up resistor: 1 kOhm for a normally-open switch (draws 5 mA only while pressed); 10 kOhm for a normally-closed switch (current flows continually); values as low as 270 Ohm advocated for noisy environments
Optional: use MCU internal pull-ups (typically 20 k to 40 kOhm on ATmega/ATtiny) when environment is quiet and leads are short
Software debounce: act on first transition, then ignore transitions until a debounce period elapses (book example: debouncePeriod = 100 with millis() tick, i.e. 100 ms)
design_notes: Pull-up value is a compromise between noise immunity and current consumption; in a noisy environment or with long switch leads, a strong external pull-up beats the weak 20-40 kOhm internal one
Swapping switch and resistor gives a pull-down wiring where a closed switch reads HIGH
Hardware debounce (e.g., a monostable that ignores subsequent pulses) is possible but software debounce reduces component count
For many buttons, a resistor ladder into one analog input saves pins; decode using value bands, not exact ADC values, because of resistor tolerance and supply variation

source.section: 13.5.1 Switches (Single Switches, Multiple Switches to One Analog Input, Debouncing)

statement: When boosting a GPIO to drive a high-power load, MOSFETs usually need no gate resistor and have exceptionally low drain-source on-resistance, letting a small MOSFET control quite big loads; but the gate is capacitive and, critically, the gate threshold voltage must sit well below the logic level or the device never turns on.
condition: Load exceeds the ~20 mA reliable GPIO drive and a discrete transistor switch (Fig. 13.21 BJT vs Fig. 13.22 MOSFET) must be chosen.
conditions: Load > ~20 mA GPIO capability: use either BJT (with base resistor) or MOSFET low-side switch
Large load current with minimal switch loss: prefer MOSFET (exceptionally low on-resistance, high off-resistance)
5 V (or lower) gate drive with a high-power MOSFET: select parts described as 'logic-level' MOSFETs, meaning gate threshold significantly less than 5 V
Strict adherence to design rules: add a gate resistor of around 1 kOhm to limit gate-charging inrush
tradeoffs: MOSFET: for most applications no gate resistor is needed; BJT always needs a base resistor
MOSFET gate is a capacitive load: inrush current on pin state changes is very high but very brief; microcontrollers generally cope
Small MOSFET can control big loads thanks to low Rds(on); equivalent BJT dissipates more
failure_modes: N-channel MOSFET with 6 V gate threshold will not turn on from a 5 V pin — common trap with high-power (non-logic-level) MOSFETs
Omitting a gate resistor leaves the GPIO exposed to the brief high gate-charging inrush (usually tolerated, violates strict design rules)

statement: If current through a relay coil, solenoid, or motor is abruptly interrupted by a mechanical or transistor switch without a transient suppressor, the collapsing magnetic field (V = L dI/dt) produces voltage spikes — a couple hundred volts even from small supplies, and as high as 1000 V — that zap transistors and switches, cause arcing that degrades switch contacts, and hammer the relay's own contacts.
condition: Inductive load (relay/solenoid/motor coil) switched off with no reverse-biased diode (DC) or RC/TVS/MOV suppressor across the coil.
consequence: Damage or destruction of the switching transistor or neighboring devices, arcing and contact degradation, erratic operation; can even shock a person touching the switch.

values.typical_spike: up to a couple hundred volts with small supply voltages

design_notes: Fix for DC coils: reverse-biased diode (e.g., 1N4004) across the coil, peak-current rated for the full coil current
The interrupting device need not be a switch — transistors and thyristors interrupting coil current cause the same spike

source.section: 2.24.12 Voltage Spikes Due to Switching; 3.4.2 A Few Notes about Relays

statement: Budget only about 20 mA of reliable source or sink current per microcontroller digital output; Arduino (ATmega) pins handle up to 40 mA per pin with a 200 mA maximum per chip, and these figures should be derated by 25 percent for a production product. Any heavier load (relay, high-power LED) requires a transistor stage.
condition: Sizing loads connected directly to MCU digital output pins (ATmega/Arduino class, 5 V).
design_notes: Atmel states the chip copes with the absolute maximum ratings as published (already derated), but the 25 percent production derating is still the book's recommendation

statement: Choose the level-conversion method by line direction: unidirectional lines (TTL serial, SPI) from a 5 V output into a 3.3 V input need only a resistor voltage divider, a 3.3 V output can drive a 5 V input directly, but bidirectional/mode-changing lines (I2C, 1-Wire) need a level-shifter IC.
condition: Interfacing a 5 V microcontroller with 3.3 V (or 1.8 V) devices over serial/bus lines; many 3.3 V devices are not 5 V tolerant.
conditions: 5 V Tx output into 3.3 V device input: resistor voltage divider required (Fig. 13.36) to prevent damage
3.3 V Tx output into 5 V MCU Rx input: connect directly — a 5 V input sees anything over about 2.5 V as logic high
I2C or 1-Wire (pins switch between input and output): use a level-shifting IC such as TXS0102; alternatives MAX3372, PCA9509, PCA9306
tradeoffs: Resistor divider: two passives, but only valid when the line direction never changes
Level-shifter IC: handles bidirectional lines and two channels (TXS0102 ideal for I2C) at the cost of an extra IC
failure_modes: Driving a non-5V-tolerant 3.3 V input straight from a 5 V Tx damages the 3.3 V device
A fixed divider on an I2C/1-Wire line breaks when the pin changes mode from input to output

statement: To measure a voltage above the MCU analog-input range, scale it with a two-resistor divider and clamp the ADC pin with a zener diode for protection; for a 0-50 V input into a 5 V ADC the divider ratio is 1:11 (not 1:10).
condition: Measured voltage exceeds the microcontroller analog input range (example given: source beyond 0-10 V up to 50 V, 5 V ADC) or may transiently exceed the expected range.
inputs: External DC voltage, 0 to 50 V in the book's example
outputs: 0-5 V scaled voltage into MCU analog input, clamped against overvoltage
required_blocks: Two-resistor voltage divider, ratio 1:11 for 50 V full scale into 5 V (remember it is 1:11, not 1:10)
Zener diode (5.1 V class) across the ADC input as overvoltage protection (Fig. 13.20)
design_notes: The zener starts to conduct before 5.1 V, degrading reading linearity near full scale — this is why the usable input range is labeled 0 to 50 V rather than 0 to 55 V
Purely resistive sensors (LDRs, thermistors) instead form one leg of a potential divider to produce the ADC voltage

statement: In a common-cathode LED display, drive each segment anode from its own MCU pin through a separate current-limiting resistor; never use one resistor on the common pin, because total current is then fixed no matter how many LEDs are lit and the display dims as more segments illuminate.
condition: Driving multi-LED packages (seven-segment or matrix displays) from microcontroller pins.

values.multiplexed_common_current: potentially eight LEDs at once — too much for most microcontroller pins

design_notes: When multiplexing multi-digit displays, switch each digit's common cathode through a transistor, since the combined current of up to eight lit LEDs exceeds MCU pin capability
Charlieplexing (n pins drive n^2 - n LEDs, e.g., 4 pins -> 12 LEDs) relies on boosted peak LED currents at low duty cycle; if the microcontroller freezes mid-refresh, the LEDs could burn out

statement: Drive a relay coil to at least within +/-25 percent of its specified control-voltage rating: too much voltage may damage or destroy the magnetic coil, too little may fail to trip the relay or make it flip back and forth erratically.
condition: Selecting supply/driver for any electromechanical relay coil.

values.typical_dc_coil_ratings: 6, 12, 24 V DC with coil resistances about 40, 160, 650 Ohm respectively
values.reed_relay: 0.2-2 ms switching, coil resistance around 250-2000 Ohm, excitation 5/6/12/24 V DC

design_notes: Coil resistance lets the synthesis agent compute coil current (e.g., 12 V / 160 Ohm = tens of mA) to size the driver transistor and flyback diode
Reed and solid-state relays are typically limited to SPST switching and tend to be damaged by power surges; mechanical relays offer SPST/SPDT/DPDT arrangements

source.section: 3.4.1 Specific Kinds of Relays; 3.4.2 A Few Notes about Relays

statement: For an AC-driven relay coil a flyback diode does not work (it conducts on alternate half-cycles, and two reverse-parallel diodes block the coil entirely); instead place a series RC network across the coil — R = 100 Ohm and C = 0.05 uF works fine for most small loads driven from the power line.
condition: Suppressing switching transients on AC-actuated relay or transformer coils.
design_notes: The capacitor absorbs excess charge and the resistor controls its discharge
Rate both R and C for a transient current as large as the typical coil current; the capacitor must be rated for AC line voltage
Discrete suppressors (bidirectional TVS, MOV) can replace the RC network

source.section: 3.4.2 A Few Notes about Relays — AC-Driven Coil; 3.4.3 AC-Actuated Switch
